name: Chestnut-leather brown
lede: Chestnut-leather brown is a dark red-brown whose Japanese library name, Kurikawacha, describes exactly that: the color of a chestnut's outer skin, and it reads only about 3 units from plain [[mahogany]].

sections.title: Kurikawacha, a chestnut's skin
sections.body:
The Wikipedia survey "Traditional colors of Japan" lists this color under the romanized name Kurikawacha, written 栗皮茶 [1]. The kanji read, in order, chestnut, skin, and brown (tea-color), and the library's own gloss, unusually, matches the English name word for word: "chestnut-leather brown" [1]. No book consulted here independently dates the name or names a dyer, so the earlier history is undocumented [1].

The nearest already-named color in our library is [[mahogany]], at a color-distance of 3.3, close enough that the two would be hard to tell apart on screen; the library also lists [[dusty-mahogany]] in the same neighborhood [1]. The hex, #60281E, is a modern screen approximation, not a measured dye or pigment [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
A color within range of this swatch is common in our archive: it appears in 1,965 of the 23,781 paintings, about 8.26 percent, as photographed; the within-painting lens finds it 897 times [2]. That makes it more common than 89 percent of the named colors we track [2].

It peaks in the 1400s, present in 61 of 945 paintings from that century, 1.7 times the expected rate [2]. Inside a painting it most often plays an accent, in roughly half the paintings that carry it [2]. Juan de Juanes is its most devoted painter, using it in 6 of his 15 works here, nearly five times his museums' baseline rate [2]. The earliest dated appearance we have is 1150, though the archive's early centuries are thin, so this is a floor and not a true first sighting; it also shares canvases with [[espresso]] and [[brownish-orange]] more often than chance would predict [2].
